chapters.title: Chapter 6: Risk Parity and Volatility-Weighted Allocation

lessons.title: Volatility Targeting: Sizing Positions by Risk, Not by Rupees

body.text: Risk parity decides how much of each asset relative to the others. It does not decide how big the whole portfolio should be at any given moment. That second, separate decision, scaling total exposure up or down to hold overall portfolio risk roughly constant as market volatility itself rises and falls, is what portfolio-level volatility targeting actually does.

children.text: Lesson 1 built risk parity's relative weighting logic. This lesson covers the separate, absolute-scale decision: choosing a target volatility, deciding how often to actually rebalance rather than just re-estimate, and an honest look at vol targeting's least discussed downside, that it cuts exposure whenever volatility rises, whether or not the move underway is actually one you would have wanted to hold through.
Two Separate Decisions: Relative Weights and Absolute Scale

Risk parity, correctly implemented, always produces weights that equalize risk contribution relative to each other, regardless of whether overall market volatility is high or low that week. It answers "how much Nifty relative to G-Sec futures," not "how much total exposure should this book be running right now." Portfolio-level volatility targeting answers the second question directly: it scales the entire book's notional exposure, leverage, up or down, so the whole portfolio's own realized volatility tracks a chosen target, even as the underlying assets' individual volatilities, and therefore the risk-parity-weighted portfolio's natural volatility, drift over time.

body.caption: Portfolio-level volatility targeting. The risk-parity base weights set relative allocation; this leverage multiplier scales the entire book up or down so total realized volatility tracks the chosen target as market conditions change.

children.text: Choosing a Target Volatility: There Is No "Correct" Number

Target volatility is a mandate and risk-tolerance decision, not something derived from theory. A conservative multi-asset systematic allocation might target somewhere in the range of 5% to 8% annualized volatility, while a more aggressive systematic book might target 10% to 15% or higher, trading off smoother returns against lower expected absolute return in rupee terms. There is no universally correct choice; it depends entirely on the capital behind the strategy and how much drawdown its investors, or its own risk committee, can genuinely tolerate without abandoning the approach at the worst possible moment, a real business constraint, not just a statistical one.
Rebalancing Frequency: The Same Noise-vs-Responsiveness Trade-off, Again

markDefs.definition: A tolerance range around the target leverage multiplier within which the portfolio does not rebalance, even though its computed target has drifted slightly. Rebalancing only happens once the drift exceeds this band, reducing unnecessary turnover from reacting to statistically insignificant day-to-day noise.

children.text: Re-estimating realized volatility daily, using Chapter 3's EWMA approach, does not mean actually trading every single day. Doing so would generate meaningful, unnecessary turnover from reacting to statistically noisy day-to-day fluctuations in the vol estimate. Standard practice uses a

: recompute the target leverage multiplier continuously, but only actually rebalance the book once the drift between current and target leverage exceeds some threshold, commonly around 10% of the target itself. This is the same fundamental trade-off Chapter 3 covered for correlation windows, applied here to when a systematic desk actually pulls the trigger on a resize.
The Perverse Side Effect: Selling Into a Vol Spike

Vol targeting is mechanically direction-agnostic: it cuts exposure whenever realized volatility rises, regardless of whether that rising volatility accompanies a crash you were glad to be smaller for, or a sharp, genuinely favorable rally you would have preferred to stay fully sized into. A fast, strong upward move in an asset you are long often comes with elevated volatility too, and a vol-targeted position will automatically shrink its exposure right in the middle of that move, giving back some of the very upside the strategy exists to capture. This is a real, honest cost of the mechanism, not a flaw specific to any poor implementation.

body.text: Vol targeting reduces tail risk on average, but it is not free. It systematically underweights fast, volatile rallies alongside fast, volatile crashes, because the mechanism responds to the magnitude of volatility, not to whether that volatility happens to be working in your favor. A desk that only markets vol targeting's downside protection, without acknowledging this upside-capping side effect, is describing half the mechanism.

children.text: Practical Implementation: EWMA Estimates, No-Trade Bands, and Leverage Caps

One more practical guardrail matters: an unusually calm period can push realized volatility very low, and the raw target-over-realized formula would then call for very high leverage, which is rarely appropriate regardless of how calm the recent past has looked. A maximum leverage cap prevents the formula from ever recommending exposure beyond what the desk's actual risk tolerance and margin capacity can support.

body.code:
target_vol = 0.10
no_trade_band = 0.10       # rebalance only if drift exceeds 10% of target leverage
max_leverage = 2.0         # hard cap, regardless of how low realized vol reads

realized_vol = ewma_vol(portfolio_returns, lam=0.94)  # Chapter 3's EWMA method
raw_leverage = target_vol / realized_vol
leverage_multiplier = min(raw_leverage, max_leverage)

drift = abs(leverage_multiplier - current_multiplier) / current_multiplier
if drift > no_trade_band:
    rebalance_to(leverage_multiplier)
# else: hold current sizing, avoiding unnecessary turnover
body.caption: A minimal practical structure: EWMA volatility estimation, a leverage cap to prevent overreaction to unusually calm periods, and a no-trade band to control turnover from statistically insignificant drift.

body.title: The Rally That Got Smaller as It Got Better
body.scenario: A vol-targeted multi-asset book runs at 1.0x leverage through a calm period, then enters a sharp, sustained equity rally driven by strong domestic flows. As the rally accelerates, realized volatility rises meaningfully alongside it, and the portfolio's leverage multiplier is automatically reduced from 1.0x to 0.6x over several weeks, per the formula in this lesson. The rally continues for two more months after the deleveraging, and the desk's realized gains from the move end up smaller than they would have been at constant 1.0x leverage.
body.prompt: Was the vol-targeting system malfunctioning? How should the desk think about this outcome?
body.modelAnswer: The system was not malfunctioning, it did exactly what vol targeting is designed to do: reduce exposure as realized volatility rises, regardless of whether that volatility is accompanying a move the desk would have preferred to stay fully sized into. This is precisely this lesson's warning about vol targeting's direction-agnostic nature. The desk should not conclude the mechanism is broken; it should recognize this as the honest, structural cost of a strategy built to reduce tail risk during crashes, which necessarily also reduces exposure during volatile rallies, since the formula cannot distinguish between the two kinds of volatility. If this trade-off proves unacceptable often enough, the appropriate response is reconsidering the target volatility level, the no-trade band, or the leverage cap, not treating a single rally's reduced capture as evidence of a bug.

body.title: Computing the Leverage Multiplier
body.prompt: A risk-parity book targets 10% annualized portfolio volatility. Its current EWMA-estimated realized portfolio volatility is 7%. What leverage multiplier should be applied to scale exposure toward the target? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 10 / 7 ≈ 1.43. Since realized volatility (7%) is currently below the target (10%), the formula calls for levering up, roughly 1.43x the base risk-parity weights, to bring the portfolio's realized volatility back up toward the 10% target.

body.title: Why Use a No-Trade Band
body.question: Why does a systematic desk typically rebalance a vol-targeted portfolio only when leverage drift exceeds a no-trade band, rather than rebalancing to the exact target every single day?
options: Because daily rebalancing is not technically possible

Because daily volatility re-estimates carry meaningful statistical noise, and rebalancing to every small, insignificant fluctuation generates unnecessary transaction costs without a corresponding risk-management benefit
Because SEBI prohibits daily portfolio rebalancing
Because a no-trade band eliminates the need to ever re-estimate volatility
body.explanation: A no-trade band exists because day-to-day changes in a volatility estimate carry real statistical noise, echoing Chapter 3's correlation estimation discussion. Rebalancing to chase every small drift generates transaction costs without a meaningful corresponding improvement in risk control, so a desk waits until the drift is large enough to be worth acting on.

points: Risk parity sets relative weights between assets; portfolio-level volatility targeting is a separate decision, scaling the entire book's exposure up or down to hold overall realized volatility near a chosen target

Target volatility is a mandate and risk-tolerance choice, not a value derived from theory, with real-world systematic allocations commonly ranging from roughly 5% to 15%+ annualized depending on risk appetite
A no-trade band avoids unnecessary turnover from rebalancing to statistically insignificant day-to-day noise in the volatility estimate
Vol targeting is mechanically direction-agnostic: it cuts exposure during volatile rallies just as it does during volatile crashes, an honest, often underemphasized cost of the mechanism
A maximum leverage cap prevents the target-over-realized formula from recommending excessive exposure during unusually calm periods
Together, risk parity and vol targeting answer two separate questions: how much of each asset relative to the others, and how large the whole book should be right now
